stories.headline: Indian markets defy global meltdown
stories.title: Indian markets defy global meltdown
stories.summary: While concerns over AI capital expenditure, chipmakers’ earnings and lofty valuations have triggered a global market sell-off, Indian equities remain relatively insulated, given their limited exposure to these risks. Unlike the US, where a handful of AI-linked stocks have dominated market performance, India’s rally has been underpinned by broader earnings growth and domestic liquidity.As worries mount over the sustainability of the AI-driven rally in developed markets, investors are increasingly reallocating capital to markets with stronger fundamental visibility. This has helped Indian benchmark indices, the Sensex and the Nifty, gain over 10 percent in the last six weeks, making India one of the standout markets amid the global turbulence. On Wednesday, the BSE Sensex and the Nifty gained around 2 percent each.In contrast, other Asian markets are on the decline. Asian technology stocks slid on Wednesday, with Japanese semiconductor stocks bearing the brunt of the sell-off, as fresh concerns about the sustainability of the AI trade spilled over from Wall Street and weighed on investor sentiment. South Korea’s Kospi slumped over 6 percent, while Japan’s Nikkei fell nearly 3 percent.“None of these issues should really affect India except from a sentiment perspective obliquely (AI versus non-AI markets). For India, earnings and oil prices will matter more,” says Sanjeev Prasad, managing director and co-head, Kotak Institutional Equities. He expects increased volatility in the near term for Indian markets, given their exposure to global investment sentiment.Also Read: Ashishkumar Chauhan: The man who transformed the marketsPrasad also notes that the Indian markets would have to contend with a sharper fall in other developed markets and emerging markets in the past month, a sharp deterioration in global risk sentiment and/or a possible resurgence of the ‘AI trade’.“We expect Indian market returns to be largely driven by crude prices in the near term and earnings in the medium term. The sharp run-up in the market and stocks across ‘consumption’ sectors in the past week would suggest that the market is already factoring in lower crude oil prices and higher margins in FY28,” Prasad elaborates.Prasad is not alone in his optimism. In November, many foreign brokerages renewed their bullish stance on India, betting on the domestic market as an alternative to AI trades. The likes of Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley, CLSA, Jefferies, Citi and HSBC have turned more constructive on Indian equities, upgrading their outlook as they see India as both a key beneficiary and diversifier in the AI era—attractive valuations and a favourable earnings growth outlook have further strengthened the investment case.Indian stocks: The new-found loveAnalysts at Goldman Sachs expect the Nifty to reach 28,500 by end-2027, driven by 15 percent earnings growth. “India’s growth has remained resilient despite US tariffs, equity portfolio outflows and the latest Middle East conflict-driven energy shock. Timely fiscal support, earlier monetary easing, and strong credit growth cushioned activity,” they say.However, as financial conditions tighten and the effects of tax cuts fade, Goldman Sachs expects real gross domestic product (GDP) growth to moderate but remain strong at 7.2 percent year-on-year in 2027, supported by a nascent recovery in the private capex cycle. The analysts are also optimistic that the worst is likely over for the rupee, which is supported by robust services exports, remittances, and improved capital flows.For Ridham Desai and Nayant Parekh, equity strategists at Morgan Stanley, Indian stocks appear to be at an inflection point and could do significantly better next year. “It is rare that growth is accelerating, valuations are relatively inexpensive and sentiment is negative. In our view, this could support higher stock prices in the coming months,” say Desai and Parekh.As markets adopted a risk-off stance in October amid uncertainty surrounding the outcome of the US midterm elections, India stood out as foreign institutional investors (FIIs) returned, even as investors pared their exposure to global equities.Also Read: Has the tide really turned for Indian markets?In early November, CLSA was among the first foreign brokerages to upgrade India to ‘overweight’, anticipating a gradual revival in investor appetite for Indian stocks. “India’s anti-AI trade label is turning from a liability into an asset,” said Alexander Redman, chief equity strategist, CLSA.Jefferies has also increased India's weighting in its Asia-Pacific ex-Japan relative-return portfolio to 15 percent, from 13.3 percent. “Financial markets continue to act like the AI capex cycle has peaked, in spite of a lack of any compelling evidence as yet of any such development on the ground. Greed and fear will continue to assume for now that the market signal is the correct one where the only issue is whether this is the peak of the cycle or a mid-cycle correction,” Christopher Wood, global head of equity strategy, Jefferies, wrote in his latest note on November 19.Desai and Parekh similarly argue that any cooling in the AI capex theme could shift investor focus to India’s stronger earnings and structural growth story. According to Desai and Parekh, India offers durable, diversified and decoupled growth—characteristics that will likely create upside potential for Indian stocks if the AI capex story wanes and/or geopolitics settle down. In any case, India's earnings growth cycle is gaining traction. They explain that this is important because a principal catalyst for India to outperform in 2027 is how the market gauges the earnings growth gap between India and the world.“High-frequency indicators look solid, underscoring an up-cycle from improving investments, monetary policy support, an undervalued currency, lack of fiscal headwinds, and robust consumer sentiment,” Desai and Parekh add.Also Read: Nifty 50 pay hikes trail inflationFIIs flock to IndiaForeign investors have poured nearly $16 billion into Indian equities since October 16, indicating a dramatic shift in sentiment after an extended period of selling. The immediate catalyst is largely external, says Prateek Ancha, chief economist, Axis Capital.“An October correction in crowded AI trades, a sharp political setback for Republicans in the November elections, and the leadership upheaval at Nvidia. Together, these developments have raised the hurdle rate for financing the next generation of US data centres. India offers diversification: A domestic-demand-led earnings base and lower direct exposure to the AI theme,” adds Ancha.FIIs sold $2.2 billion worth of Indian equities in October, lower than the outflows recorded in the previous month. In contrast, domestic institutional investors (DIIs) invested $6.3 billion, extending their strong buying momentum for the 39th consecutive month.Meanwhile, an analysis by Axis Capital shows that, as foreign equity flows have turned positive since mid-October, India’s outperformance relative to emerging-market peers has lifted its benchmark weight by 4 percentage points.“Equity valuations appear inexpensive, cycle-adjusted, relative to history,” say Desai and Parekh. They feel that the earnings cycle has resumed its upward journey, helped by an emerging private capex cycle, the releveraging of corporate balance sheets, a robust banking system, improving terms of trade (via both a higher share in global trade and a lower share of oil in GDP) and the unfolding of a structural rise in discretionary consumption.Analysts at Goldman Sachs explain their bullish stance on India. After a $64 billion peak-to-trough FII selloff, foreign ownership sits at its lowest level in more than a decade. “Since the mid-October bottom, India has received the largest share of foreign inflows within the EM pack. Valuations have de-rated significantly from peak levels, close to their 10-year average,” they say.Even as India’s earnings prospects and growth momentum are drawing foreign investors back to local stocks, there are some concerns over underlying inflation.India's retail inflation pushed past the Reserve Bank of India’s upper tolerance limit in October, with the headline rate climbing to 6.1 percent from 5.5 percent in September. This is the first breach of the 6 percent ceiling in the new Consumer Price Index (CPI) series. Food and beverages inflation accelerated to 8.5 percent from 7.4 percent. Vegetable inflation jumped to 10.9 percent, the highest in the new series, even as wholesale vegetable prices began to cool.While Goldman Sachs economists expect real GDP growth to moderate to 7.2 percent year-on-year in 2027 (from 7.9 percent year-on-year in 2026), they “expect above-consensus headline inflation of 5.7 percent YoY in 2027, amid El-Niño-related weather disruptions and high input costs, driving the view that there should be further monetary tightening ahead.”Desai and Parekh of Morgan Stanley also agree that, from a policy perspective, there is hardly anything wrong with the Indian economy except for some upside risk to inflation. “While we see far-reaching reforms that could lift growth rates in the coming quarters, policymakers could also roll out policies to directly alleviate the pain in equities,” they explain.

opening: While concerns over AI capital expenditure, chipmakers’ earnings and lofty valuations have triggered a global market sell-off, Indian equities remain relatively insulated, given their limited exposure to these risks.
Unlike the US, where a handful of AI-linked stocks have dominated market performance, India’s rally has been underpinned by broader earnings growth and domestic liquidity.
body: As worries mount over the sustainability of the AI-driven rally in developed markets, investors are increasingly reallocating capital to markets with stronger fundamental visibility.
This has helped Indian benchmark indices, the Sensex and the Nifty, gain over 10 percent in the last six weeks, making India one of the standout markets amid the global turbulence.
In contrast, other Asian markets are on the decline.

Asian technology stocks slid on Wednesday, with Japanese semiconductor stocks bearing the brunt of the sell-off, as fresh concerns about the sustainability of the AI trade spilled over from Wall Street and weighed on investor sentiment.
South Korea’s Kospi slumped over 6 percent, while Japan’s Nikkei fell nearly 3 percent.
“None of these issues should really affect India except from a sentiment perspective obliquely (AI versus non-AI markets).
For India, earnings and oil prices will matter more,” says Sanjeev Prasad, managing director and co-head, Kotak Institutional Equities.
He expects increased volatility in the near term for Indian markets, given their exposure to global investment sentiment.

Prasad also notes that the Indian markets would have to contend with a sharper fall in other developed markets and emerging markets in the past month, a sharp deterioration in global risk sentiment and/or a possible resurgence of the ‘AI trade’.
“We expect Indian market returns to be largely driven by crude prices in the near term and earnings in the medium term.

The sharp run-up in the market and stocks across ‘consumption’ sectors in the past week would suggest that the market is already factoring in lower crude oil prices and higher margins in FY28,” Prasad elaborates.
Prasad is not alone in his optimism.
In November, many foreign brokerages renewed their bullish stance on India, betting on the domestic market as an alternative to AI trades.

The likes of Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley, CLSA, Jefferies, Citi and HSBC have turned more constructive on Indian equities, upgrading their outlook as they see India as both a key beneficiary and diversifier in the AI era—attractive valuations and a favourable earnings growth outlook have further strengthened the investment case.
“India’s growth has remained resilient despite US tariffs, equity portfolio outflows and the latest Middle East conflict-driven energy shock.
Timely fiscal support, earlier monetary easing, and strong credit growth cushioned activity,” they say.

However, as financial conditions tighten and the effects of tax cuts fade, Goldman Sachs expects real gross domestic product (GDP) growth to moderate but remain strong at 7.2 percent year-on-year in 2027, supported by a nascent recovery in the private capex cycle.
The analysts are also optimistic that the worst is likely over for the rupee, which is supported by robust services exports, remittances, and improved capital flows.
For Ridham Desai and Nayant Parekh, equity strategists at Morgan Stanley, Indian stocks appear to be at an inflection point and could do significantly better next year.
“It is rare that growth is accelerating, valuations are relatively inexpensive and sentiment is negative.
In our view, this could support higher stock prices in the coming months,” say Desai and Parekh.

As markets adopted a risk-off stance in October amid uncertainty surrounding the outcome of the US midterm elections, India stood out as foreign institutional investors (FIIs) returned, even as investors pared their exposure to global equities.
“India’s anti-AI trade label is turning from a liability into an asset,” said Alexander Redman, chief equity strategist, CLSA.
Jefferies has also increased India's weighting in its Asia-Pacific ex-Japan relative-return portfolio to 15 percent, from 13.3 percent.
“Financial markets continue to act like the AI capex cycle has peaked, in spite of a lack of any compelling evidence as yet of any such development on the ground.

Greed and fear will continue to assume for now that the market signal is the correct one where the only issue is whether this is the peak of the cycle or a mid-cycle correction,” Christopher Wood, global head of equity strategy, Jefferies, wrote in his latest note on November 19.
Desai and Parekh similarly argue that any cooling in the AI capex theme could shift investor focus to India’s stronger earnings and structural growth story.

According to Desai and Parekh, India offers durable, diversified and decoupled growth—characteristics that will likely create upside potential for Indian stocks if the AI capex story wanes and/or geopolitics settle down.
In any case, India's earnings growth cycle is gaining traction.
They explain that this is important because a principal catalyst for India to outperform in 2027 is how the market gauges the earnings growth gap between India and the world.

“High-frequency indicators look solid, underscoring an up-cycle from improving investments, monetary policy support, an undervalued currency, lack of fiscal headwinds, and robust consumer sentiment,” Desai and Parekh add.
Foreign investors have poured nearly $16 billion into Indian equities since October 16, indicating a dramatic shift in sentiment after an extended period of selling.
The immediate catalyst is largely external, says Prateek Ancha, chief economist, Axis Capital.
“An October correction in crowded AI trades, a sharp political setback for Republicans in the November elections, and the leadership upheaval at Nvidia.
Together, these developments have raised the hurdle rate for financing the next generation of US data centres.
India offers diversification: A domestic-demand-led earnings base and lower direct exposure to the AI theme,” adds Ancha.

Meanwhile, an analysis by Axis Capital shows that, as foreign equity flows have turned positive since mid-October, India’s outperformance relative to emerging-market peers has lifted its benchmark weight by 4 percentage points.
“Equity valuations appear inexpensive, cycle-adjusted, relative to history,” say Desai and Parekh.

They feel that the earnings cycle has resumed its upward journey, helped by an emerging private capex cycle, the releveraging of corporate balance sheets, a robust banking system, improving terms of trade (via both a higher share in global trade and a lower share of oil in GDP) and the unfolding of a structural rise in discretionary consumption.
Analysts at Goldman Sachs explain their bullish stance on India.
“Since the mid-October bottom, India has received the largest share of foreign inflows within the EM pack.
Valuations have de-rated significantly from peak levels, close to their 10-year average,” they say.
Even as India’s earnings prospects and growth momentum are drawing foreign investors back to local stocks, there are some concerns over underlying inflation.
This is the first breach of the 6 percent ceiling in the new Consumer Price Index (CPI) series.
Food and beverages inflation accelerated to 8.5 percent from 7.4 percent.
“While we see far-reaching reforms that could lift growth rates in the coming quarters, policymakers could also roll out policies to directly alleviate the pain in equities,” they explain.

stories.headline: Trump's tariff threat: Why US is taking aim at Make in India, Atmanirbhar Bharat
stories.title: Trump's tariff threat: Why US is taking aim at Make in India, Atmanirbhar Bharat
stories.summary: Trump's tariff threat: Why US is taking aim at Make in India, Atmanirbhar Bharat
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: The US Trade Representative has determined that India's acts, policies and practices relating to structural excess capacity and production are "unreasonable" and burden or restrict US commerce.
It has proposed tariffs of up to 25 per cent on Indian goods, to which New Delhi has responded by rejecting the charge.
India is expanding factories, strengthening supply chains and developing domestic industries to increase its manufacturing capacity and establish itself as a major global manufacturing hub.

Make in India, Atmanirbhar Bharat (Self-Reliant India) and the Production Linked Incentive (PLI) schemes have been central to that push, with New Delhi offering incentives to bring investment home, expand production and reduce dependence on imports.
But the Donald Trump administration took a very different reading of these policies.

Washington is arguing that India's drive for self-reliance risks producing too much manufacturing capacity and output, particularly when domestic demand does not keep pace with the factories being built.
That, US officials say, can push Indian companies towards export markets, where they compete with American manufacturers.
The Trump administration has used this argument to justify imposing tariffs on India.

The US Trade Representative has determined that India's acts, policies and practices relating to structural excess capacity and production are "unreasonable" and burden or restrict US commerce under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974.
It also claimed that a range of India's industrial and trade practices contribute to "structural excess capacity and production" and has proposed tariffs of up to 25 per cent on Indian goods.
The rate could be lowered to 17 per cent if the two countries reach a qualifying trade agreement.
That puts some of India's most prominent economic initiatives -- from Make in India and PLI to Self-Reliant India -- at the centre of a new trade confrontation.

stories.headline: CJI calls for greater representation to women in legal profession
stories.title: CJI calls for greater representation to women in legal profession
stories.summary: Chief Justice of India Justice Surya Kant called for at least one-third women juniors in senior advocates' chambers and more women panel lawyers at the Shashi Prabha Singh Memorial Awards.

article_sentences: Chief Justice of India Justice Surya Kant called for at least one-third women juniors in senior advocates' chambers and more women panel lawyers at the Shashi Prabha Singh Memorial Awards.

New Delhi: Chief Justice of India Justice Surya Kant has called for greater representation of women in the legal profession, asking senior advocates to ensure that at least one-third of junior lawyers in their chambers are women.

Addressing the inaugural Shashi Prabha Singh Memorial Awards ceremony at the Siri Fort Sports Complex here, the CJI on Wednesday also stressed the need to appoint more women as panel lawyers to strengthen their participation and representation at the Bar.

The awards, instituted in memory of the late mother of senior advocate and former Supreme Court Bar Association president Vikas Singh, were presented to four young women advocates in recognition of their potential and contributions to litigation.
The initiative also aims to provide financial assistance to help them advance their legal careers.
The CJI underscored the imperative to create equitable opportunities for women in the legal profession.
He urged that every senior advocate engaging juniors should ensure that at least one out of every three juniors in their chambers is a woman advocate.
Lawyer Monika Dhiman received the Nyaya Prabha Ratna award, while Huma Anjum and Priyanshi Kumari were jointly honoured with the Nyaya Prabha Gaurav award.
Lawyer Kavana Rao received the Nyaya Prabha Samman.

stories.headline: Sheshnag: Kashmir’s Sacred Lake Under Threat
stories.title: Sheshnag: Kashmir’s Sacred Lake Under Threat
stories.summary: At 3,590 metres (about 11,780 feet), Sheshnag Lake is far more than a halt on the Amarnath pilgrimage. It anchors the ecology of the entire Liddar valley in south Kashmir. Set high in the upper reaches of Pahalgam in Anantnag district, this fragile alpine lake is fed by meltwater from the Kolahoi and Sheshnag glaciers. Its outflow becomes the Liddar river, which supplies clean drinking water to Pahalgam, Bijbehara, Anantnag and hundreds of villages before it joins the Jhelum. Kashmir’s orchards, paddy and tourism economy all depend on this mountain water system. Yet earthmovers, JCBs and bulldozers are now digging and widening a road along the very edge of this delicate ecosystem. Video and photographs of machines cutting into the lake’s banks have triggered sharp reactions across the Valley. Young people and trekkers have protested peacefully on Srinagar’s Shankaracharya hill, and thousands have signed online petitions. Political parties, religious leaders and environmental groups such as the Jammu and Kashmir Climate Action Group are demanding that the excavation stop immediately and that the project’s environmental clearances be made public. The Border Roads Organisation argues that widening the route is necessary to ease traffic, make the yatra smoother and strengthen safety. But the real question is whether a pilgrimage can be made convenient by gambling with the very nature that gives the journey its meaning. Science says it cannot. A recent study in Scientific Reports found that about 16.2 percent of the Baltal-Amarnath corridor falls in the highly landslide-prone category, while 68.1 percent is moderately susceptible. Researchers analysed 49 major landslides in the corridor, and 71.4 percent of them occurred in zones already rated highly susceptible. Most striking, 60 to 70 percent of the mapped slope failures lay within 50 metres of roads, tracks or other human intervention. When slopes steeper than 25 degrees are cut with heavy machinery, the rock loses its natural grip, and rain or snowmelt can then bring the hillside down. Sheshnag’s geology magnifies the danger. The lake rests on natural embankments of loose rock, soil and debris left by glaciers over thousands of years, known as moraines, along with permafrost. It is among the 14 high-risk glacial lakes identified by the Jammu and Kashmir administration, where a glacial lake outburst flood is a real threat. Excavation in its catchment can weaken those moraine dams. If debris or boulders slide into the lake, the water level can surge and breach the natural barrier. The floods from South Lhonak Lake in Sikkim and from glacial lakes in Nepal showed how quickly meddling in the high Himalaya can sweep away everything downstream. Climate data deepen the concern. Weather records for the Baltal-Amarnath region show average temperatures rising by roughly 2°C in recent decades, with a steady increase of about 0.05°C a year. Between 1994 and 2024, the valley recorded 54 extreme rainfall events, days with more than 45 millimetres of rain. The July 2022 cloudburst near the Amarnath cave, and the deluge of debris that killed pilgrims, is still fresh in public memory. Geologists, including Prof. Shakil Ahmad Romshoo, vice chancellor of the Islamic University of Science and Technology, have documented the rapid retreat of the Kolahoi glacier. Black carbon from heavy machinery and vehicles settles on snow and ice, absorbing more solar heat and speeding up melting. Ecologically, Sheshnag is an oligotrophic lake: low in nutrients and rich in dissolved oxygen. Such high-altitude lakes have very little capacity to cleanse themselves. Soil and construction debris from hill-cutting that enters the water settles as silt, reducing the lake’s depth and storage capacity and destroying aquatic life and alpine vegetation. If the lake’s water system is contaminated, the damage will fall directly on the drinking water and farming of Pahalgam and Anantnag. Millions of families with no link to the pilgrimage business would suffer. Uttarakhand’s experience is a living, bitter warning. The Kedarnath disaster and the land subsidence in Joshimath proved that the young, brittle Himalayan mountains have a limited carrying capacity. When that limit is breached in the name of development and tourism, nature restores its own balance, and humans pay the price. After those tragedies, Uttarakhand’s administration was compelled to cap pilgrim numbers in sensitive areas and restrict mechanised construction near glaciers. The Supreme Court and the National Green Tribunal have repeatedly invoked the precautionary principle, directing that any infrastructure in the high Himalaya must first undergo a transparent, independent environmental impact assessment. Before pushing Kashmir toward a Joshimath or Kedarnath of its own, policymakers must rethink their priorities. The safety and ease of pilgrims matter, but the answer does not lie in indiscriminate road widening and bulldozers on a lake’s shore. A controlled, eco-friendly model, as in the Swiss Alps, is possible: limited entry, natural protection of footpaths, relocation of temporary camps to landslide-free sites, and options such as ropeways in the most sensitive stretches. The government should halt all mechanised digging in and around Sheshnag at once, and commission a committee of independent glacier experts and ecologists to assess the whole area scientifically. A road built by hollowing out our water sources and the foundations of our mountains is not progress. It is a path to self-destruction. Pankaj Chaturvedi, Senior Journalist & Environmentalist

After those tragedies, Uttarakhand’s administration was compelled to cap pilgrim numbers in sensitive areas and restrict mechanised construction near glaciers.

The Supreme Court and the National Green Tribunal have repeatedly invoked the precautionary principle, directing that any infrastructure in the high Himalaya must first undergo a transparent, independent environmental impact assessment.
Before pushing Kashmir toward a Joshimath or Kedarnath of its own, policymakers must rethink their priorities.
The safety and ease of pilgrims matter, but the answer does not lie in indiscriminate road widening and bulldozers on a lake’s shore.

A controlled, eco-friendly model, as in the Swiss Alps, is possible: limited entry, natural protection of footpaths, relocation of temporary camps to landslide-free sites, and options such as ropeways in the most sensitive stretches.
The government should halt all mechanised digging in and around Sheshnag at once, and commission a committee of independent glacier experts and ecologists to assess the whole area scientifically.
A road built by hollowing out our water sources and the foundations of our mountains is not progress.
It is a path to self-destruction.
Pankaj Chaturvedi, Senior Journalist & Environmentalist.

sentences.text: The floods from South Lhonak Lake in Sikkim and from glacial lakes in Nepal showed how quickly meddling in the high Himalaya can sweep away everything downstream.
Weather records for the Baltal-Amarnath region show average temperatures rising by roughly 2°C in recent decades, with a steady increase of about 0.05°C a year.
It is among the 14 high-risk glacial lakes identified by the Jammu and Kashmir administration, where a glacial lake outburst flood is a real threat.
At 3,590 metres (about 11,780 feet), Sheshnag Lake is far more than a halt on the Amarnath pilgrimage.

stories.title: Supreme Court's Sabarimala verdict due before Christmas; Knanaya endogamy case deferred as ruling may have a bearing
stories.summary: The Supreme Court indicated that the Sabarimala reference verdict could come before the Christmas break and deferred the Knanaya Church’s endogamy case to January 2027.
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
event term: 'supreme court' in summary weight 26.4
article_sentences: Kasaragod: The Supreme Court on Wednesday indicated that its verdict in the Sabarimala reference on women's entry into the hill shrine would be delivered before the Christmas break.

The indication came while the apex court was hearing a challenge by the Knanaya Catholic Church against a Kerala High Court judgment that struck down the Church's practice of enforcing endogamy by excluding members who marry outside the community.
The Bench deferred the Knanaya petitions, observing that the Sabarimala ruling could have a bearing on the issues involved.

A three-judge Bench of Justices B V Nagarathna, R Mahadevan and Sanjeev Sachdeva deferred the Knanaya petitions to January 5, 2027, indicating that they would be considered after the nine-judge Constitution Bench delivers its verdict in the Sabarimala reference.

Justice B V Nagarathna said that the Sabarimala verdict was likely to be delivered before the Supreme Court closes for its Christmas vacation on December 18, Adv Sai Shashank, who represents the reformist group in the Knanaya case, told Onmanorama.
The nine-judge Bench had reserved its judgment on May 14 after 16 days of hearings.
The Sabarimala reference, however, goes beyond the question of women’s entry into the hill shrine.
Several other disputes involving religious practices and the rights of religious denominations have been tagged with the reference for consideration by the larger Bench, said Adv Shashank.

These include challenges concerning the entry of Muslim women into mosques and dargahs, the exclusion of Parsi women from fire temples after marrying outside the community, and the practice of female genital mutilation among the Dawoodi Bohra community.
The reference also encompasses the Dawoodi Bohra community’s power to excommunicate members, he said.

The larger Bench is examining constitutional questions on the scope of religious freedom under Articles 25 and 26 of the Constitution, the autonomy of religious denominations, the limits of judicial scrutiny of religious practices and the relationship between individual rights and denominational rights.

The Knanaya dispute raises a closely related question: whether a religious community can invoke its right to manage its own affairs to enforce endogamy, or whether an individual’s right to choose a spouse takes precedence.

stories.headline: US proposes 25 per cent tariffs on India; 17 per cent if trade deal clinched
stories.title: US proposes 25 per cent tariffs on India; 17 per cent if trade deal clinched
stories.summary: Washington, Nov 25: The US on Wednesday proposed 25 per cent tariffs on Indian goods in the absence of a trade deal, citing excess industrial capacity, sustained market access barriers and inadequate labour protection that harm American companies. The US Trade Representative (USTR) said the tariffs on India would amount to 17 per cent if it agrees to a trade deal with America. The fresh tariff proposal follows Section 301 investigations launched by the USTR in March targeting 16 economic jurisdictions. The USTR proposed tariffs of up to 20 per cent to 35 per cent on other targeted economies, though lower rates apply to trading partners with deals in place. The EU, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and Switzerland face 15 per cent tariff rates, inclusive of standard import duties. Vietnam would face tariffs of 20 per cent if the trade deal is finalised. “For decades, many of our trading partners have adopted industrial strategies built on targeting manufacturing, wage and labour suppression, financial and other support, non-market economy inputs, and other market-distorting practices that tilt the trade balance in their favour while eroding America's manufacturing base,” said USTR Jamieson Greer. “India generates trade surpluses in sectors such as pharmaceuticals, steel, and ICT goods, revealing dependencies on Indian manufacturing in certain key sectors,” the USTR said in its report on ‘India's Acts, Policies, and Practices Relating to Structural Excess Capacity and Production in Manufacturing Sectors’. These new tariffs would not be added to existing ones aimed at combating forced labour or certain sector-specific tariffs, a senior US official said. The USTR has decided to schedule public hearings on its proposals on January 25 and sought written comments from interested persons by January 5. The Office of the USTR has been analysing for several months whether 16 jurisdictions have policies that favour surplus production, a practice that drives down prices and harms US industry. The investigation began last March, after the Supreme Court overturned the indiscriminate trade levies imposed by the Trump administration invoking the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA). After that reversal, the USTR opened two investigations based on Article 301: one directed at 60 jurisdictions (about a hundred countries) for violating export regulations on forced labour; and the other against 16 jurisdictions for promoting surplus production. India and the US are negotiating an interim bilateral trade agreement after the framework they had finalised in February went back to the discussion board with the Supreme Court striking down the IEEPA tariffs imposed last year. India is seeking lower tariffs for its goods in the US market than its competitors such as Bangladesh, Vietnam and Cambodia. “USTR is applying to India a diagnosis built for a very different economy. India consumes most of what it produces and buys more goods from the world than it sells, so it is not exporting a domestic glut,” said Abhik Sengupta, a Task Force Observer on the Committee on Strategic Trade and Market Access, Helsinki Geoeconomics Society. Sengupta said India’s reliance on Chinese inputs points to gaps in its industrial base, not a surplus. “Penalising India for closing those gaps risks pushing supply chains back toward the very economies Washington is most concerned about,” he said.

stories.headline: A commitment to strengthen our Constitution
stories.title: A commitment to strengthen our Constitution
stories.summary: On 26th November 1949, the Constituent Assembly adopted our Constitution. Today, we remember Dr. Rajendra Prasad, Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar and every member of the Constituent Assembly. Their greatness lay in drawing extensively from the rich traditions and civilisational wisdom of Bharat while framing a modern Constitution. For a nation as diverse as Bharat, with its numerous faiths, languages, customs and schools of thought, it is important that the Constitution have a resonance far beyond the precincts of Parliament and the courts. Our endeavour has been to deepen its connect with the collective consciousness of our people, especially our youth and strengthen the spirit of unity essential to India’s bright future. That is why over a decade ago, our Government decided to mark 26th November as Constitution Day. For crores of Indians, including me, the Constitution of India is an inseparable part of our life journeys. Whenever I look back at my childhood, the humble circumstances in which I grew up, the struggles that were a part of everyday life, I am filled with an overwhelming sense of gratitude towards our Constitution. That a child born into a family of modest means, with no privileges or advantages of birth, could one day be entrusted with the responsibility of serving the world’s largest democracy speaks volumes about how extraordinary our Constitution is. It is due to our Constitution that circumstances of one’s birth no longer determine the limits of one’s future. In our own humble way, we have sought to repay this debt of gratitude by strengthening our Constitution. The distinguished constitutional scholar Granville Austin described our Constitution as “ first and foremost a social document.” The quest for social and economic justice runs through the very fabric of our Constitution. Thus, what can be more satisfying than working towards the realisation of this cherished vision of the makers of our Constitution? A recent World Bank report highlights that nearly 50 crore Indians have moved out of poverty. Breaking free from generations of deprivation, crores of parents can now dream of a better future for their children. When PM Awas Yojana ensures a family moves from a thatched roof to a pucca home, the constitutional promise of dignity acquires meaning. When Ujjwala Yojana frees a mother from the hardships of a smoke-filled kitchen, we advance the ideals of equality and well-being. When Ayushman Bharat enables a poor family to access quality healthcare without the fear of debt, social justice becomes a lived reality. When MUDRA and PM-SVANidhi provide collateral-free credit to small entrepreneurs and street vendors, economic justice finds expression. When digital technology and platforms like UPI transcend all divides and place opportunities once available to a privileged few within the reach of every citizen, we advance the constitutional ideal of inclusivity. There are many more manifestations of this constitutional vision. The list of amendments we brought can be viewed through the same prism. The 101st Amendment ushered in GST, a long-awaited reform. The 102nd Amendment granted constitutional status to the National Commission for Backward Classes, fulfilling a long-standing dream of the marginalised sections of society. The 103rd Amendment received broad social acceptance. By providing reservation to Economically Weaker Sections, it addressed the long-overlooked aspirations of economically disadvantaged families from communities outside the existing reservation framework. For the first time since 1950, an updated version of our Constitution is now available in all 22 languages of the Eighth Schedule. This has brought our Constitution closer to the people. Even after our Constitution came into force in 1950, we continued to be governed by the colonial penal code dating back to the 1860s. With the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, we have sought to bring about a fundamental shift in our criminal justice system, moving from the colonial emphasis on punishment (Dand) to a citizen-centric pursuit of justice (Nyay). Over the past decade, we have laid special emphasis on Kartavya, or the duties of a citizen. Our civilisation has always emphasised the responsibilities that accompany every role in society. The spirit of Kartavya has found expression in several mass movements, from Swachh Bharat to water conservation and environmental protection. However, there is another reality that I feel compelled to share. There have been occasions in our history when those entrusted with upholding the Constitution chose to weaken it. Ironically, they are the same people who had the opportunity to govern India for five decades. This year marks 75 years since the First Amendment of 1951, when a government that was not popularly elected used its majority in the Provisional Parliament to restrict fundamental freedoms. Its timing, barely months before India’s first general election, proves that it was intended to influence the electoral process and stifle public opposition. It is also 50 years since the 42nd Amendment at the height of the Emergency. This curtailed judicial review and fundamentally altered the balance of institutional powers. I would also urge youngsters to study the 38th and 39th Amendments to know what a power-hungry and anti-constitutional leadership can do. The repeated misuse of Article 356 to dismiss elected state governments presents another troubling chapter. One party has the dubious record of imposing Article 356 almost a hundred times and one former Prime Minister has scored a half-century in this field. The makers of our Constitution had hoped that it would be implemented in letter and spirit across India. But, for over 70 years, Articles 370 and 35A did not allow the full Constitution to be implemented in Jammu and Kashmir, thus trampling over the rights of SC, ST, OBC communities and women. It was only in 2019 that this historical wrong was corrected. For decades, in several parts of India, particularly in tribal areas, Naxalites used the might of the gun to deny the poorest people the rights guaranteed to them by our Constitution. The successful elimination of Naxalism this year is particularly heartwarming because it has ensured that the poorest of the poor can finally exercise their constitutional rights without fear. Now, we are left only with ‘Dimagi Naxals’, far removed from the realities of our times but persistent in their efforts to derail our growth trajectory. It is most appalling that the biggest party in the Opposition wants to reduce OBC reservation and bring Muslim reservations, something the makers of our Constitution, notably Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar, were totally against. The journey of our Constitution would be incomplete without recognising the remarkable women who helped shape it. But what happened earlier this year should fill our hearts with shame. A legislation aimed at giving women adequate representation in legislative bodies was disallowed from being passed by the one Opposition party, once again showing its disdain for constitutional values. I assure the Nari Shakti of India that no force can prevent us from ensuring that justice is done to them. Our constitutional democracy has a clearly defined role for the Opposition. Sadly, the leading Opposition party seems to have become more of an Avrodh Paksh (obstructionist) than a Virodh Paksh (opposition). They should know that disrupting democratic processes is no substitute for discharging constitutional responsibilities. Today, India stands at a defining moment. As we work towards Viksit Bharat by 2047, two simple yet powerful principles can guide our collective endeavours: India First in our thinking and Kartavya (Duties) in our actions. With these as our guiding principles and the Constitution as our source of strength, we can secure a bright future for generations to come. Shri Narendra Modi, Honourable Prime Minister of India

stories.headline: Cabinet approves ₹2,014-crore greenfield airport at Silchar
stories.title: Cabinet approves ₹2,014-crore greenfield airport at Silchar
stories.summary: AAI to develop airport at Doloo to overcome capacity constraints at the existing civil enclave
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'cabinet approves' in title weight 44
article_sentences: To overcome operational and capacity constraints at Silchar’s existing airport, the Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs (CCEA) on Wednesday approved the development of a greenfield airport at Doloo in Assam at an estimated cost of ₹2,014 crore.
Accordingly, the new airport will be developed by the Airports Authority of India (AAI) to cater to the growing passenger traffic in South Assam and adjoining areas of neighbouring States.
The current passenger traffic is served by a civil enclave on defence land, which faces severe operational and spatial constraints, limiting its ability to accommodate sustained passenger growth.

Consequently, on Wednesday, the CCEA, chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, approved the project, which includes a terminal building spread over 12,351 square metres with the capacity to handle 800 passengers during peak hours.
Besides modern passenger amenities, the terminal will incorporate green building principles and provision for modular expansion.
Furthermore, the airport will have a 2,705-metre-long and 45-metre-wide runway compliant with Code 4C standards and suitable for Airbus.
A320 aircraft operations.
Additionally, the project includes an apron capable of parking six.
A320 aircraft and a dedicated isolation bay.
Located in Assam’s Cachar district, Doloo forms part of the Barak Valley, which has extensive tea gardens, agro-based industries and potential for eco and cultural tourism.

In addition, the airport will ease pressure on existing infrastructure and support regional trade and tourism, while strengthening the region’s connectivity with the broader national and international aviation network.

stories.headline: Supreme Court Grants Bail To 3 Former Rajasthan PHED Officials In ₹979 Crore Jal Jeevan Mission Tender Scam
stories.title: Supreme Court Grants Bail To 3 Former Rajasthan PHED Officials In ₹979 Crore Jal Jeevan Mission Tender Scam
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: The Supreme Court on Wednesday (November 25) granted bail to three former senior officials of Rajasthan's Public Health Engineering Department (PHED), accused of facilitating the alleged award of tenders worth approximately ₹979.45 crore under the Jal Jeevan Mission through forged work-experience certificates.

A bench of Justice Dipankar Datta and Justice Sheel Nagu allowed the appeals filed by former Additional Chief Secretary and PHED Finance Committee Chairman Subodh Agarwal, former Chief Engineer Dinesh Goel, and former Superintending Engineer Mahendra Prakash Soni, setting aside the Rajasthan High Court's orders rejecting their bail pleas.
The Court noted that the investigation against the appellants had concluded and chargesheets had been filed.
It also took into account that the trial was likely to be prolonged, given the voluminous documentary evidence and the proposed examination of 124 witnesses.
Charges were yet to be framed.

The bench observed that keeping the accused in further pre-trial custody would serve no useful purpose, particularly when several co-accused, including the then Rajasthan PHED Minister Mahesh Chandra Joshi, had already been granted bail.
The Court reiterated that the seriousness of the allegations in an economic offence cannot, by itself, justify prolonged incarceration of an undertrial.
“Pre-trial incarceration cannot masquerade as punitive detention.” the Court observed, referring to its earlier order granting bail to co-accused persons in the case.

It added that although the allegations of institutional collusion in a public welfare project were grave, their severity could not operate as an absolute bar to bail or justify keeping an accused in custody when there was no prospect of an early conclusion of the trial.
The case arose from allegations of large-scale irregularities in the implementation of the Jal Jeevan Mission in Rajasthan.

According to the prosecution, between 2021 and 2023, two private contracting firms, M/s Shri Ganpati Tubewell Company and M/s Shri Shyam Tubewell Company, allegedly obtained forged work-experience certificates purportedly issued by IRCON International Limited.
Using these certificates, the firms allegedly secured work orders in approximately 104 tenders worth ₹979.45 crore, in connivance with senior public servants.
